content.text: Topic 3.17 showed that some problems cannot be solved in a REASONABLE amount of time — the algorithm exists but is too slow for large inputs. Topic 3.18 goes further: some problems cannot be solved CORRECTLY for all inputs by ANY algorithm, no matter how much time you give it. These are called undecidable problems. This is not a limitation of current technology — it is a fundamental, mathematically proven boundary of what computation can do.

content.label: Big Idea
content.text: There exist problems that computers cannot solve, and even when a computer can solve a problem, it may not be able to do so in a reasonable amount of time. Topic 3.18 addresses the first part: problems that computers CANNOT solve at all — not slow, not impractical, but mathematically impossible.

content.definition: A decision problem for which an algorithm can be written to produce a correct output for all inputs. Example: Is the number even?

content.text: Most problems we encounter in computing are decidable. A decidable problem is one where we can write an algorithm that always produces a correct yes or no answer for every possible input — no matter what input you give it, the algorithm terminates with the right answer.

content.definition: A problem for which no algorithm can be constructed that is always capable of providing a correct yes-or-no answer. An undecidable problem may have some instances with an algorithmic solution, but no single algorithm can solve all instances.

content.text: An undecidable problem is NOT just a hard problem. It is NOT just a slow problem. It is a problem for which mathematicians have PROVEN that no algorithm can EVER exist that always gives a correct answer for all possible inputs. This proof is mathematical — it is not a statement about current technology or computing power, and no future computer or technology can change it.
The Halting Problem: The Classic Example

The most famous undecidable problem is the Halting Problem. It asks: given any program and any input to that program, will the program eventually stop running (halt), or will it run forever (enter an infinite loop)? This seems like a question a computer should be able to answer by analyzing the code. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no algorithm can correctly answer this question for all possible programs and inputs.

content.text: A Critical Nuance: Some Instances May Be Solvable

content.definition:
Decidable: an algorithm exists that always produces a correct yes/no answer for all inputs.
Undecidable: no algorithm can always produce a correct yes/no answer for all inputs. Some instances may be solvable but not all.

content.text: An undecidable problem may have some instances that have an algorithmic solution, but there is no algorithmic solution that could solve ALL instances of the problem. This is one of the most important and commonly misunderstood nuances about undecidability. 'Undecidable' does NOT mean 'no instance can ever be solved.' It means 'no SINGLE GENERAL algorithm can solve ALL instances.'

Does ANY arbitrary program halt for ANY arbitrary input?
No — undecidable

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Undecidable means no single algorithm can handle ALL instances. Some specific instances of an undecidable problem may be trivially solvable — we can easily tell that 'DISPLAY hello' halts. The undecidability means we cannot write ONE algorithm that correctly handles every possible program as input. Some inputs will always defeat any algorithm we could write.
Students frequently confuse undecidable problems with problems that have unreasonable running time. These are fundamentally different concepts and must not be confused on the exam.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Students often think undecidable problems will be solved by more powerful computers. This is WRONG. Undecidability is a mathematical property — proven by mathematical logic, not dependent on hardware. A quantum computer, a hypothetical infinitely fast computer, or any future technology cannot solve an undecidable problem for all inputs. It is mathematically impossible, not just currently impractical. This is completely different from unreasonable running time, where faster hardware DOES help (though never enough for large inputs).
Scope: What Is and Is Not Tested

The CED includes an important exclusion statement: determining whether a given problem is undecidable is outside the scope of this course and the AP exam. You will NOT be asked to prove that a specific problem is undecidable. You WILL be asked to explain what undecidability means, describe the difference between decidable and undecidable problems, and understand the key nuance that some instances of an undecidable problem may have algorithmic solutions.

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Three things the AP exam tests about undecidability: (1) A decidable problem has an algorithm that always produces correct yes/no for ALL inputs. (2) An undecidable problem has NO algorithm that can always produce correct yes/no for ALL inputs. (3) Some SPECIFIC INSTANCES of an undecidable problem may be solvable — the issue is that no SINGLE algorithm works for ALL instances. The Halting Problem is the classic example. Determining whether a given problem is undecidable is NOT tested.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam
